summary: A 1977 revision of the Telnet byte macro option, which lets one side send a short code that stands for a longer string of characters. It replaces RFC 729 and is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A shortcut that types a whole sentence. This is the improved version of the rule for sending those shortcuts.

questions: what is the telnet byte macro option
how does telnet bm option work
subtitle: A Telnet option that lets one side define a single byte as shorthand for a longer string.

tldr.problem: Telnet subcommands cost at least five bytes each, which is too much overhead when data comes in tiny blocks that each need a separator mark.
tldr.mechanism: After negotiating the BM option (code 19), the sending side defines single macro bytes that stand for replacement strings. The receiver expands each macro byte as if the full string had arrived.
tldr.outcome: It works as a simple form of data compression. RFC 735 revises and obsoletes RFC 729.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 735 as a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 729. No RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Byte Macros
sections.content:
Telnet subcommands need at least five characters on the network (IAC SB, the option name, IAC SE). That is tolerable for rare subcommands, but not for block-oriented data that needs a block separator. If blocks are only five or ten bytes, most of the traffic would be control information.

The BM (byte macro) option, command code 19, is intended as a simple data compression technique that removes this overhead.
sections.eli5: If every tiny message needs a long label, the labels end up bigger than the messages. A shortcut makes the label tiny.

sections.title: Negotiating the Option
sections.content:
The option is enabled through the standard Telnet option negotiation. IAC WILL BM offers to send single data characters that stand for replacement strings, and IAC DO BM agrees to receive them. WON'T BM or DON'T BM refuses and discards any existing macro definitions. The default is WON'T BM and DON'T BM, with no reinterpretation of data bytes.

The side that sent WILL BM is free to define and use mappings. Apart from refusing particular definitions, the receiver has no control over them.
sections.eli5: First both sides say "yes, let's use shortcuts." If either says no, everyone goes back to sending every word in full.

sections.title: Defining and Using Macros
sections.content:
A sender defines a macro with IAC SB BM DEFINE macro-byte count replacement-string IAC SE. The macro byte may be any 8-bit value except IAC (decimal 255). The receiver answers with ACCEPT or REFUSE plus a reason, and the sender must not use or redefine that byte until it has an answer. Later the macro byte is sent instead of the string, and the receiver must behave exactly as if the string had been received.

No replacement happens inside a Telnet command, and expanded strings are not reinterpreted, so recursive definitions cannot be made. LITERAL marks a macro byte as real data, and PLEASE CANCEL lets the receiver ask the sender to cancel a definition. The RFC recommends choosing macro bytes from the range between decimal 128 and decimal 254, which is not normally used.
sections.eli5: You announce "this one symbol means that whole phrase." The listener says OK or no thanks. After that, each time they see the symbol they read the whole phrase.

items.label: DEFINE
items.desc: Sender defines a macro byte, a count and its replacement string.

items.label: REFUSE
items.desc: Receiver refuses, with a reason code.

items.label: LITERAL
items.desc: Treat the macro byte as real data.
